title: Interval List Intersections
description: Brute force to optimized: checking every pair across two lists versus a two-pointer merge-style sweep exploiting sortedness.

blocks.text: Problem Summary: Given two lists of closed intervals, firstList and secondList, where each list is pairwise disjoint (no two intervals in the same list overlap) and sorted, return the intersection of these two interval lists: every interval that lies in both lists.

blocks.text: Since both lists are individually sorted and internally non-overlapping, comparing the current interval from each list at a time (using two pointers) is enough to find every intersection: whichever current interval ends first can no longer intersect any LATER interval in the other list, so its pointer should advance.

blocks.title: Analogy: Finding Overlapping Time Slots Between Two People's Calendars
blocks.text: Picture two people's calendars, each individually free of double-bookings and listed in time order, and wanting every overlapping time slot between them. Walking through both calendars simultaneously with one pointer each, computing the overlap of the current two slots and advancing whichever one finishes first, finds every overlap in a single sweep.

blocks.caption: Two pointers, one per list; record overlaps and advance whichever interval ends first

blocks.text: Result: [[1,2],[5,5],[8,10],[15,23],[24,24],[25,25]], every pairwise overlap between the two lists.

Before checking every pair of intervals across both lists, notice that since both lists are individually sorted, a two-pointer sweep (one pointer per list) can find every intersection in a single linear pass, advancing whichever current interval ends first since it can no longer intersect anything further along in the other list.

blocks.title: Building the Intuition
blocks.text:
Observation 1: The overlap between two intervals [a1,a2] and [b1,b2] is [max(a1,b1), min(a2,b2)], valid only if max(a1,b1) <= min(a2,b2).

Observation 2: Since both lists are sorted and internally disjoint, once the current interval from one list ends BEFORE the current interval from the other, it cannot possibly intersect any FUTURE interval from the other list either (since those start even later).

Observation 3: This means advancing the pointer whose current interval ends earlier is always safe and never misses a potential intersection.

Observation 4: Repeating "compute overlap, advance the earlier-ending pointer" until either list is exhausted correctly finds every intersection in O(n+m) total steps.

This leads to a two-pointer sweep: at each step, compute the overlap between the current intervals from both lists (recording it if valid), then advance whichever pointer's current interval ends first.
Check every pair of intervals across the two lists directly, recording their overlap whenever one exists.

items: For every interval in firstList, compare it against every interval in secondList.
Compute their overlap as [max(starts), min(ends)]; if valid (start <= end), record it.
Collect all such valid overlaps across every pair.

blocks.text: Why the code is written this way

items: Checking every pair directly implements the overlap definition, correct regardless of order.
This costs O(n times m), unnecessary once the sorted structure allows a two-pointer approach.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n times m), n and m being the two list lengths.
Space: O(1) extra beyond the output.
Limitation: since both lists are sorted and internally disjoint, a two-pointer sweep finds every intersection in O(n+m) instead of O(n times m).

blocks.title: The Optimization Journey
blocks.text:
Why checking every pair is unnecessary: since both lists are sorted, once the current interval in one list ends before the current interval in the other, it is impossible for it to intersect anything LATER in the other list either.

The two-pointer sweep: maintain one pointer into each list; at each step, compute the overlap of the two current intervals, recording it if valid; then advance whichever pointer's current interval has the SMALLER end value, since it is now guaranteed exhausted for future comparisons.

Why this never misses an intersection: the interval NOT advanced still has a chance to overlap with subsequent intervals from the other list, so it correctly remains in play for the next comparison.

The core idea: a merge-style two-pointer sweep, exploiting that both lists are sorted and internally non-overlapping.

Maintain pointers i (into firstList) and j (into secondList). At each step, compute the overlap of firstList[i] and secondList[j], recording it if valid. Advance i if firstList[i] ends before secondList[j], otherwise advance j. Repeat until either list is exhausted.

blocks.caption: Two pointers sweep both lists once, recording overlaps and advancing the earlier-ending interval

blocks.text: Because both lists are individually sorted and internally disjoint, once the current interval from one list ends before the current interval from the other, every subsequent interval in that first list starts even later, meaning it can never overlap the still-active interval from the other list. Advancing that pointer therefore never skips a possible intersection, while the interval that ends later remains available to be compared against upcoming intervals from the other list, guaranteeing every intersection is found exactly once.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n+m), a single combined sweep through both lists.
Space: O(1) extra beyond the output.

blocks.text: Checking every pair costs O(n times m) time; the two-pointer sweep costs O(n+m) time, both using O(1) extra space beyond the output.

items: Pattern: a two-pointer merge-style sweep over two sorted, internally disjoint interval lists.
Core Idea: compute the overlap of the current two intervals; advance the pointer whose interval ends earlier, since it cannot intersect anything further ahead.
Time: O(n times m) for checking every pair, O(n+m) for the two-pointer sweep.
Space: O(1) extra for both, beyond the output.
Most Important Observation: the earlier-ending interval can safely be advanced past, since sortedness guarantees it cannot intersect anything later in the other list.
Interview Difficulty: a clean, well-known two-pointer application to interval problems.
One line memory trick: two pointers; record overlap; advance whichever interval ends first.
